title: What Your Revenue Cycle Metrics Aren’t Telling You
summary: Useful Revenue Cycle metrics do more than report performance—they explain what changed, reveal root causes, and point leaders toward the next decision.
body_markdown:
*Leaders need reporting that explains performance, reveals root causes, and points to the next decision*


**By Vanessa Couch-Laguana, Head of RCM, LunaBill**


---


Reporting performance is not the same as explaining performance. A useful metric should reveal what changed, why it changed, and who needs to act.


## We have plenty of data—but not always the right insight


Revenue Cycle leaders live and breathe total AR, days in AR, cash collections, and high-dollar worklists. We review them every day and every week, and we constantly shift team priorities to make sure the work gets done.


Those measures matter, but they can keep us stuck in the detail. They tell us what the number is without always telling us why it changed, what pattern is developing, or which stakeholder needs to act. We may know that cash missed goal or that days in AR increased, but not whether the cause was payer delay, authorization failure, late charges, unsigned notes, pricing setup, coordination of benefits, or a combination of issues.


## A monthly summary should explain the month


At the end of the month, leaders need more than a scorecard showing whether each target was met. They need a summary of what the month actually looked like. What were the top denials and rejects? Which trends appeared by payer? What should be escalated to managed care or placed on a JOC agenda? What requires VP or CFO support?


That summary should include both internal and external causes. Organizations sometimes focus heavily on payer behavior while turning a blind eye to their own process failures. That weakens the ability to challenge payers and leaves preventable defects unresolved.


## Measure internal reliability as seriously as payer performance


A useful leadership package should show point-of-service collection performance, eligibility and insurance accuracy, coordination-of-benefits issues, authorization timeliness, open documentation, late charges, pricing or supply setup delays, and other internal breakdowns that affect claim submission and payment.


Authorization is a particularly important example. Organizations need to know which services and levels of care require authorization, whether the approved span covers the entire stay, and whether added procedures or changes in care created a new requirement. Responsibility must be clear. Otherwise, departments throw the work over the fence and the failure appears later as a denial.


## Pair team intelligence with analytics


Peer-group meetings allow employees to surface emerging payer issues. Analytics should then validate the pattern quickly. The analyst should provide claim volume, dollars at risk, payments received on comparable claims, average delay, oldest and highest-dollar claims, location or specialty concentration, and the relevant contract deadline.


The report should lead to an action: continue individual follow-up, pause work while a pattern is analyzed, escalate through managed care, add the issue to the JOC agenda, correct an internal workflow, or request executive support. If a report cannot support a decision, it may be creating information without creating value.


## Redefine productivity in an automated environment


Productivity standards vary widely. One organization may expect 25 to 30 accounts per day while another expects seven or eight per hour. Neither number is meaningful without understanding system design, automation, claim complexity, manual steps, and the quality of the work.


It is difficult to hold a team to a gold standard when the system works against them. As automation removes routine clicks, leaders should shift toward resolution quality, appropriate escalation, revenue impact, and the complexity of work completed. The objective is not to reward the largest number of touches. It is to reward work that moves accounts toward the right outcome.
